sections.title: How does the Degree of unsaturation calculator work?
sections.html:
The Degree of unsaturation calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports number of hydrogen atoms (H) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in number of carbon atoms (C), number of nitrogen atoms (N), number of halogens atoms (X) and the degree of unsaturation (DoU).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Degree of unsaturation calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Number of hydrogen atoms (H)=-2 × degree of unsaturation (DoU) + 2 × number of carbon atoms (C) − number of halogens atoms (X) + number of nitrogen atoms (N) + 2

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Number of carbon atoms (C) = 10, Number of nitrogen atoms (N) = 10, Number of halogens atoms (X) = 10 and Degree of unsaturation (DoU) = 10. The calculator returns Number of hydrogen atoms (H) = 2.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Number of hydrogen atoms (H) = 2 should be roughly the size you expected from Number of carbon atoms (C) = 10 and Number of nitrogen atoms (N) = 10.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Degree of unsaturation calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Working through a stoichiometry problem
  • Converting between the units a protocol and your bench equipment use
  • Preparing a solution and checking the numbers first
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — number of carbon atoms, number of nitrogen atoms and number of halogens atoms — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Degree of unsaturation calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — number of carbon atoms for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Re-enter the same figure and confirm the result is stable; a number that moves when you press Calculate again is a sign that a field is still empty.

faq.q: What does the Degree of unsaturation calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns number of hydrogen atoms (H), derived from number of carbon atoms, number of nitrogen atoms and number of halogens atoms. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Degree of unsaturation calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for number of carbon atoms, number of nitrogen atoms, number of halogens atoms and the degree of unsaturation, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Number of hydrogen atoms (H) = 2. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Degree of unsaturation calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
